statement: A bus carries five times as many students as teachers. At a stop, 12 students get off and 3 teachers get on. Now there are twice as many students as teachers. How many students were on the bus at first?

choices.misconception: I found the number of teachers at the start and gave that instead of the number of students.
I forgot that 12 students got off, so I only added the 3 teachers to my equation.
I reversed the second sentence and wrote the teachers as twice the students.
I forgot that 3 teachers got on, so I only took the 12 students off in my equation.

hints: Call the number of teachers at the start t.
Write the starting students in terms of t, then write both new numbers after the stop. The last sentence gives one equation relating them, and the question wants students, not teachers.
Students after the stop: 5t - 12. Teachers after: t + 3. Set 5t - 12 equal to 2(t + 3).

solutions.reliable: Let there be t teachers and 5t students at first. After the stop there are 5t - 12 students and t + 3 teachers, and 5t - 12 = 2(t + 3) = 2t + 6. So 3t = 18 and t = 6, which means 30 students at first. Check: 18 students and 9 teachers after the stop, and 18 is twice 9. The transferable idea: name one unknown, write every quantity in terms of it, and re-read which quantity is asked for.
solutions.elegant: Test the choices as starting student numbers: 30 means 6 teachers, then 18 students and 9 teachers, which fits at once.

whyOnTest: Translating a two-stage story into one equation is the skill, and the distractors are what each dropped or reversed phrase produces.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
